title: Agentic Automation of BT-RADS Scoring Using an End-to-End System for Standardized Glioma Follow-up Assessment.
desc: [Radiology. Artificial intelligence] The Brain Tumor Reporting and Data System (BT-RADS) standardizes posttreatment MRI response assessment in patients with diffuse gliomas but requires complex integration of imaging trends, medication effects, and radiation timing. An end-to-end multiagent large language model and convolutional neural network system for automated BTRADS classification was developed and evaluated. Five hundred nine consecutive posttreatment glioma MRI examinations (March 2017-July 2021) from a single center were retrospectively evaluated. An extractor agent identified clinical variables from notes using gpt-oss (OpenAI, 20-billion parameters). A scorer agent applied BTRADS decision logic integrating these with quantitative volumetrics. System accuracy was compared against initial assessments, using expert annotation as the reference standard. Four hundred ninety-two examinations were evaluable. Overall system accuracy was 76.0% (374/492) versus 57.5% (283/492) for initial assessments, an absolute difference of +18.5 percentage points (P < .001). Cohen kappa between the system and the reference standard was 0.71. The system achieved high sensitivity in context-dependent categories (BT-1b; 100%; BT-1a, 92.7%; BT-3a, 87.5%) and moderate sensitivity for threshold-dependent categories (BT-3c, 74.8%; BT-2, 69.2%; BT-4, 69.3%; BT-3b, 57.1%). The BT-4 positive predictive value was 92.9%. These results support further evaluation of this system as a clinical decision-support tool, with local open-weight inference preserving data privacy.

title: Deep Learning and Engineered Biomaterials-Enhanced Imaging-Guided Cancer Immunotherapy.
desc: [Advanced healthcare materials] The clinical success of immunotherapies is hindered by the absence of robust methodologies for the early and accurate assessment of antitumor immune responses. Integrating engineered biomaterials with artificial intelligence (AI)-driven molecular imaging technology offers a powerful approach for predicting immune efficacy. However, its clinical translation is significantly hindered by several critical limitations, including the complex and costly synthesis of multifunctional imaging probes, insufficient deep-tissue penetration, suboptimal in vivo signal-to-noise ratios, potential immunogenicity and off-target toxicity, and the limited generalizability of deep learning models across heterogeneous patient populations. In view of these pressing scientific challenges, this review focuses on the application of chemical and biomolecular strategies-enhanced engineered biomaterials in promoting the sensitivity and specificity of advanced imaging modalities for visualizing signaling molecules and immune cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Meanwhile, recent progress in deep learning-driven image analysis has enabled strong predictive capabilities and automated the understanding of complex immune system dynamics. Together, these technologies provide a transformative platform for non-invasive monitoring, personalized treatment, and response prediction, with the potential to advance precision immuno-oncology and significantly impact both basic research and clinical translation.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Initiated Clinical Decision Support in Hospitalist Practice
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Cedars-Sinai Medical Center; conditions: Clinical Decision Support; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 20; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This study will evaluate the feasibility of using artificial intelligence (AI)-generated clinical decision support during routine inpatient hospital medicine care. Participating hospitalist physicians may receive AI-generated recommendations for eligible hospitalized patients under their care. Eligible patient cases will be randomly assigned to one of three AI prompting strategies that differ in the clinical information provided to the AI system. After reviewing each recommendation, participating physicians will complete a brief survey assessing the clinical usefulness of the recommendation, how they interpreted it, and whether it was or will be incorporated into patient management. The study will assess whether AI-generated recommendations can be successfully generated and delivered during routine clinical care and whether physicians complete the study surveys and adopt the recommendations. It will also provide preliminary information about physicians' perceptions of AI-generated recommendations across the three prompting strategies. The findings will be used to inform the design of a future larger randomized trial of AI-initiated clinical decision support.

title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data
desc: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI for In-Hospital Detection of Lung Cancer and Heart Failure Using Routine Data: Development, Internal Validation, and Simulated Federated Evaluation
desc: Objective: To determine whether combining four routine data sources improves in-hospital detection of lung cancer and heart failure, which sources drive each prediction, whether explanations are faithful, whether models are fair, and how much benefit federated training retains. Methods: In this retrospective single-centre study, we linked MIMIC-IV admissions (73,637 patients) to chest radiographs, radiology reports, 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) and laboratory tests from the first 48 hours. For each disease, excluding prior cases, we compared single-source models, gradient boosting and early, late and attention-based fusion on patient-level splits. We tested explanations for faithfulness and weight dependence, audited performance by sex, age, race and ethnicity, and insurance, and simulated five unequal hospitals to compare federated, centralised and local training. Results: Lung cancer was coded in 1.7% and heart failure in 15.6% of patients. For lung cancer, attention fusion reached an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of 0.833 (95% CI 0.809-0.859) against 0.753 for gradient boosting on laboratory data; for heart failure, 0.885 (0.878-0.892) against 0.794 (both p < 0.001). Early and late fusion performed similarly. Laboratory data and radiology reports contributed most to lung cancer, and the ECG to heart failure. Explanations passed a deletion test; a weight-randomisation check on absolute attributions passed for ECG but not for laboratory explanations. For heart failure, discrimination fell with age. Federated training recovered 95% of the centralised gain over local training for heart failure; for lung cancer, federated averaging (FedAvg) recovered 51% and FedProx 82%. Conclusion: Fusing routine data improved in-hospital detection of both diseases over laboratory data alone, and which data matter depends on the disease. Explanation checks should be run per source and per similarity measure, and performance in older patients monitored. For the rare outcome, FedProx, which limits drift between sites, retained more of the pooled benefit than FedAvg. External validation is needed.

title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
desc: Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Framework for Early- versus Late-Stage Classification of Breast Cancer from Gene Expression, with Co-expression Network Analysis
desc: Anatomical stage is a principal determinant of treatment and prognosis in breast cancer, yet it is unclear how much information about stage is carried by the transcriptome of the primary tumour. We asked whether an a priori panel of 65 cancer-related genes can distinguish early-stage (AJCC Stage I-II) from late-stage (Stage III-IV) breast cancer, and which genes contribute to any signal. RNA-seq expression and pathologic stage for The Cancer Genome Atlas breast invasive carcinoma cohort (TCGA-BRCA) were obtained from the UCSC Xena platform. After restricting the data to primary tumours with a known stage, 1,075 tumours were analysed (805 early, 270 late) and split into stratified training (n = 860) and held-out test (n = 215) sets. Logistic regression, a support vector machine, random forest and gradient boosting were tuned by stratified five-fold cross-validation, with median imputation, standardisation and SMOTE oversampling fitted on training data only and classification thresholds chosen on out-of-fold training predictions. On the test set, Logistic Regression had the highest ROC-AUC, 0.618 (95% CI 0.530-0.704), with balanced accuracy 0.578, sensitivity 0.741 and specificity 0.416; differences in AUC between models were not statistically significant (DeLong p = 0.199-0.585). Permutation importance in the Gradient Boosting model ranked POU5F1, FLT3 and NOTCH1 highest, but this model's AUC confidence interval included 0.5, so the ranking is exploratory. No gene was differentially expressed between stage groups after false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction (smallest FDR = 0.057, CD44). A co-expression network built from training tumours identified REL, EP300 and ESR1 as the most connected genes, a property that reflects co-expression rather than regulation or association with stage. Limitations include a single cohort, no external validation, no clinical covariates and a small number of late-stage test tumours. Expression of this gene panel carries limited but measurable information about anatomical stage; expression-based stage models should be combined with clinicopathological variables and validated in independent cohorts before any clinical application is considered.

title: Lymph node-targeted, mKRAS-specific amphiphile vaccine in pancreatic cancer: the randomized phase 2 AMPLIFY-7P trial
desc: Camupepimut (ELI-002 7P) drives mutated KRAS (mKRAS)-specific T cell responses that correlated with disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) in patients with mKRAS pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) in the phase 1 AMPLIFY-201 trial. In the phase 2 AMPLIFY-7P trial, patients with stage I-III KRAS-mutated PDAC without recurrence within 6 months of standard therapy were randomized 2:1 to camupepimut (n = 96) or standard-of-care/observation (n = 48). Stratification balanced nodal status. The primary DFS endpoint was not met (median 23.8 versus 21.2 months; HR 0.85, P = 0.5329). However, prespecified and exploratory analyses were informative. A numerical DFS advantage at 6 months of 14.0% (75.7% versus 61.7%; HR 0.55, P = 0.0557) corresponded to camupepimut dosing. Post hoc multivariate Cox regression analysis of DFS indicated an improved outcome for camupepimut (adjusted HR 0.47, P = 0.0086), a worse outcome for stage III disease (adjusted HR 2.29, P = 0.0127), an elevated baseline CA19-9 (adjusted HR 3.16, P 9.17-fold over baseline (82.2%, 74/90) correlated with improved DFS (HR 0.22, P < 0.0001), with the median DFS not reached versus 6.08 months for above and below 9.17-fold, respectively. Camupepimut safety was similar to observation, with grade ≥3 adverse events in 10.4% (10/96) versus 14.6% (7/48), and few serious AEs (6.3%, 6/96 versus 8.3%, 4/48; reflecting progression/surgical complication). These efficacy and immunogenicity signals will inform a refined strategy for a confirmatory phase 3 trial. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05726864.

title: Association of ambient artificial intelligence scribe availability with patient instruction documentation and readability in ambulatory care.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] This retrospective cohort study evaluated the effect of an artificial intelligence (AI) scribe on patient instructions documentation in ambulatory internal medicine settings. We analyzed 391 061 adult encounters at a single medical center from December 2023 to July 2025. A difference-in-differences analysis estimated the relationship of AI scribe availability with patient instructions documentation frequency. Mixed-effects logistic regression estimated the association between encounter-level AI scribe utilization and documentation, adjusted for patient, clinician, and encounter characteristics. Length and readability were compared across instructions created by AI alone, clinicians assisted by AI, and clinicians alone. Character-level edit distances between AI drafts and final documentation were calculated. AI scribe availability was associated with a 10.5 percentage-point increase in patient instructions documentation frequency (P = .018), and encounter-level AI use was associated with higher odds of documentation (aOR 4.32; 95% CI, 4.14-4.50). AI instructions were longer than clinician-authored content (median 1994 vs 482 characters) and scored higher on 3 text-complexity indices (all P < .001). Clinician editing of AI content increased length without meaningfully reducing complexity. AI drafts and final documentation differed substantially, with a median character-level edit distance of 39.7%. AI scribe availability was associated with increased patient instructions documentation. However, AI-generated instructions were longer and scored as more linguistically complex than clinician-authored instructions, and clinician editing did not close this gap. Ambient AI scribes can improve availability but may increase complexity of patient instructions. Research into downstream effects including patient comprehension and satisfaction is warranted.

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Parasitology: A holistic perspective from diagnosis to therapeutics.
desc: [Experimental parasitology] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated to address challenges in parasite detection, disease surveillance, and therapeutic development. This narrative review examines current and emerging AI applications in parasitology across diagnostics, drug discovery, genomics, epidemiology, education, and public health decision-making, with particular emphasis on diagnostic applications. Machine learning and deep learning methods support automated parasite detection, classification, and quantification in microscopic images, alongside medical image analysis and arthropod identification. Applications are discussed for malaria, leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, cystic echinococcosis, soil-transmitted helminth infections, and intestinal protozoal infections. Beyond diagnosis, AI-assisted approaches support compound screening, drug repurposing, toxicity prediction, and prioritization of potential therapeutic targets. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses also offer opportunities to investigate parasite biology and predict drug resistance. Surveillance models may inform outbreak forecasting and targeted control, although their operational value requires evaluation in the intended settings. Educational applications remain emerging, and the benefits of digital learning should be distinguished from those attributable specifically to AI. Across these domains, performance on curated datasets does not establish clinical utility or generalizability. Major barriers include limited representative datasets, insufficient external and prospective validation, infrastructure constraints, and concerns regarding privacy, bias, and accountability. Future progress requires reproducible evaluation, experimental validation of therapeutic candidates, and assessment of clinical and public health benefits. AI is therefore best positioned as a complementary tool that supports parasitological expertise, with responsible implementation guided by transparency, equitable access, and human oversight.

title: Machine Learning to Predict Fever After Labor Analgesia
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Chengdu Jinjiang Maternity and Child Health Hospital; conditions: Intrapartum Fever; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 6144; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Post-labor analgesia intrapartum fever (PAIF) is a serious complication that increases the risk of cesarean delivery, postpartum bleeding, and health problems for newborns. Currently, doctors lack a simple tool to predict which mothers will develop a fever before they start labor analgesia. This study aims to develop and test a computer prediction tool (using machine learning) to estimate the risk of PAIF. The investigators will review the medical records of mothers who received labor analgesia and delivered at term in three hospitals in China. Information that is available before the mothers receive analgesia, such as maternal age, gestational age, blood test results, and labor progress, will be collected. Using artificial intelligence, the investigators will build a prediction model. This model will then be tested on a separate group of women from a different hospital to ensure it works well in different settings. Finally, an open-access, interactive online calculator will be developed for clinicians. The goal of this study is to provide doctors with a practical tool to quickly assess a mother's risk level before starting analgesia. This will help doctors monitor high-risk mothers more closely and prepare for possible complications. This study only uses existing medical records and will not change the routine care of any patients. Further studies will be needed to see if using this tool improves the health of mothers and babies.

title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of the Patient-Artificial Intelligence Rating Instrument
desc: Importance: Patients increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) for health-related conversations, but evaluation measures largely reflect clinician judgment. Objective: To develop and preliminarily evaluate a patient instrument assessing the quality of patient-AI health conversations. Design: Cross-sectional survey conducted June 5-14, 2026, following patient-partnered instrument development and cognitive interviews. Setting: An anonymous online survey. Participants: A convenience sample of adults with prior use of large language models for personal health-related queries, recruited from an academic medical center-affiliated Insight Panel and patient peers. Exposures: Participants' own prior health-related conversations with AI tools of their choosing. Main Outcomes and Measures: The Patient-AI Rating instrument comprised 12 communication-quality and patient engagement items rated from 1 to 5 and a separately scored patient-perceived-harm item. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach alpha, with sensitivity analyses using first ratings only for those using the tool to rate multiple conversations and participant-mean profiles. We examined item-total correlations, inter-item structure, and between- and within-participant variation. Results: Fourteen participants contributed 46 complete ratings; among 13 providing demographics, median age was 63 years (IQR, 53-70 years), and 8 (62%) reported female gender. Participants provided a median of 2 ratings (range, 1-17). Cronbach alpha was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.83-0.93) across all ratings, 0.85 using first ratings only, and 0.92 using participant-mean profiles. Corrected item-total correlations ranged from 0.42 to 0.72; mean inter-item correlation was 0.40. No item deletion improved Cronbach alpha. The mean quality score was 4.43 (SD, 0.45). Among 9 participants contributing multiple ratings, the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.45, suggesting inter-conversation variability. No perceived harm was reported in 44 of 46 ratings (96%); the harm item correlated minimally with the instrument total (r = 0.09). Conclusions and Relevance: In this small cross-sectional study of engaged patients, the Patient-AI Rating instrument showed promising internal consistency and variation across rated conversations. These findings support further evaluation of patient-reported communication quality alongside clinician-based measures. title: PRET is a few-shot system for pan-cancer recognition without example training
desc: Pathological examination stands as the cornerstone in cancer diagnosis, impacting millions worldwide annually. With the shortage of pathologists globally, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged rapidly to automate the diagnostics process. However, conventional AI models require substantial labeled data for each disease, posing huge challenges in scalability and practicality. Therefore, we introduce PRET (pan-cancer recognition without examples training), a few-shot system to achieve flexible, scalable, and effective cancer recognition across diverse organs, hospitals and tasks without training. Evaluated on 23 international benchmarks comprising 4,484 whole-slide images, our method outperforms existing approaches across 20 tasks, achieving over 97% area under the curve on 15 benchmarks with a maximum improvement of 36.76%. title: BUDDY: An interactive web platform to accelerate the functional modeling of human missense variants using Saccharomyces cerevisiae orthologs
desc: The advent of next-generation sequencing has transformed clinical genetics, accelerating the identification of human genetic variants. However, the labor-intensive process of functional validation of Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS) remains a significant diagnostic barrier. While expressing humanized genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a common approach for modeling missense variants with functional assays, using native yeast orthologs provides a more streamlined approach that preserves species-specific interactions within multisubunit complexes. However, taking this approach relies on a fragmented workflow that requires bioinformatic experience. To address this issue, we developed the Bioinformatic Utility for Diagnostic Discovery in Yeast (BUDDY), an integrated web platform designed to streamline variant analysis by connecting bioinformatic tools and databases including ClinVar. Features include amino acid alignments, a protein structure viewer that displays a superposition of yeast and human proteins, pathogenicity prediction data, CRISPR-Cas9 reagent design, and yeast phenotypes to provide potential functional assays. The platform also contains an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted experimental design feature that evaluates the utility of modeling specific variant and gene combinations in yeast and can assist with phenotype selection. BUDDY significantly accelerated the bioinformatic preparation time needed for ortholog variant modeling by an experienced biologist. Additionally, without prior bioinformatics training, a first-year medical student used BUDDY to develop a self-directed project and proposed a study of five Lynch syndrome-associated VUS using a forward mutation rate assay. BUDDY is designed to accelerate the investigation of human variants in yeast and has a high potential utility for use in resource-constrained settings such as course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs).

title: Agentic artificial intelligence for code status extraction from clinical notes: a cross-model comparison of single agent, reflective agent, and multiagent extractor-reviewer system.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To evaluate whether increasing agentic architectural complexity via self-reflection or multiagent design improves clinical code status extraction (Do Not Resuscitate [DNR], Do Not Intubate [DNI], Comfort Measures Only [CMO]) across open-source large language models (LLMs) of varying capabilities. We conducted a controlled cross-model comparison evaluating 3 architectures: (1) single extractor agent, (2) single agent with self-reflection, and (3) sequential multiagent extractor-reviewer system. Four open-source LLMs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B) were evaluated on 1000 Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV-Note discharge summaries. Ground truth labels were established through a physician-AI dual review with adjudication (Cohen's κ = 0.98-0.99). Models were evaluated on accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Cohen's κ, token consumption, and processing latency. McNemar's test was used for paired comparisons. For capable larger models (GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B), single-agent architectures achieved comparable or superior performance for explicit code status (DNR, DNI) relative to complex systems, whereas multiagent review doubled token consumption and latency without accuracy gains. Reflective self-review significantly impaired MedGemma-27B-IT on DNI extraction (P = .047). For the smaller DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, multiagent review provided statistically significant corrective benefits for DNR (P = .017) and CMO (P < .001), demonstrating a capability-threshold effect, though performance remained below clinically acceptable levels. Architectural complexity does not enhance extraction performance for capable LLMs, and reflective self-review may cause conservative overcorrection. Multiagent verification value is inversely related to model capability. Single-agent LLMs provide optimal accuracy and efficiency for explicit clinical extraction in capable models. Agentic complexity must be matched to both task characteristics and model capability rather than adopted by default.
